1.4.2 Behavioural measures

To get a single net placement location estimate per trial and participant (net placement center), we calculated the circular mean of the positions of the placed mosquito nets (0–7 nets) per trial and participant. Angles were wrapped … to avoid …  Error is the absolute circular distance in degree(°) between the placement centre and the hidden-state target. As described above, the hidden-state target is the center of the von Mises distribution and thus contains no outcome noise, unlike the observed attack direction. Analyses of how net placement centers were updated across trials use the observed attack direction. To compare placements across the two color cues, each participant’s learned cue-2 offset was subtracted from cue-2 placements. The offset was estimated, per episode, as the difference between the circular mean placements for the two cues on regular trials from the fourth trial of the episode onward, and averaged across episodes.

Net placements around each event are indexed as follows. The event trial (t0) is the trial in which the mosquito nets were placed before observing that the direction of the mosquito attack has shifted. The net placement in the event trial thus reflects a pre-event baseline. The first net placement after the displaced mosquito attack is t+1. The first net placement after the next attack is t+2; it is the first net placement at which an oddball and an episode transition can be distinguished – for an oddball, the target angle at t0 equals the target angle at t+2; for an episode transition, the target angle at t+1 equals the target angle at t+2. The following placement is t+3. After a transition, error is computed relative to the target angle of the new latent state, and after an oddball relative to the unchanged target angle.

Net entropy is the Shannon entropy, in bits, of the net allocation of the 7 nets over the 32 positions. It is 0 bits when all nets are stacked on one position and 2.81 bits when they occupy seven different positions, so that higher values indicate a wider spread of net allocation within a single trial.

Alternative models.
Four alternative models were specified to test whether behaviour required latent-state inference (

): nets placed at random positions; a single direction tracked by a delta rule without distinguishing the colour cues; the same with a learned cue offset; and an agent that knows both directions of each cue and covers both on every trial without inferring which state is active.
Estimation.
Parameters and model probabilities were estimated by amortized simulation-based inference with BayesFlow 2.0 (
Radev et al., 2023

). Each session was summarized by 54 behavioural features describing the spread of the allocation, accuracy and interception, the trial-to-trial change of the placement, the responses to oddballs and episode transitions, and the use of the colour cues (

The posterior network (flow matching with a summary network) was trained on 100,000 sessions simulated with parameters drawn from the priors on the 20 trial schedules of the study, for 150 epochs; for each participant, 4,000 posterior samples were drawn. The model classifier was trained on 100,000 sessions simulated from the five models in equal proportions, for 200 epochs, and returns the posterior probability of each model for a participant’s session.
1.5 Statistical Analysis
Statistical analyses were conducted in Python (version) and R/RStudio (version).

Trial- and episode-level data were analyzed with linear mixed-effects models (LMM) fitted by restricted maximum likelihood (REML) in lme4 and lmerTest, with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom. Proportions (beta distribution) and binary outcomes (binomial distribution) were modelled with generalized linear mixed models in glmmTMB (ref), tested with Wald z-tests. Model terms are reported as Type III F-tests.

Instruction condition was entered in every model as an unordered factor with two orthogonal, sum-to-zero planned contrasts. The first compares participants told the structure with those not told it (C3 versus the mean of C1 and C2, weights −1/3, −1/3, 2/3); the second compares participants told that rules exist with those told nothing (C2 versus C1, weights −1/2, 1/2, 0). With this coding, all other terms of a model are evaluated as the unweighted mean over the three conditions. Condition differences are reported as contrasts of the estimated marginal means (emmeans package in RStudio; ref), which average over the covariates of a model. Model coefficients are reported instead for interactions of condition with trial-level predictors, where they equal the difference between the contrasted conditions in the effect of that predictor. Planned contrasts are reported unadjusted. All pairwise condition comparisons are reported with Holm correction.

Random effects followed the design of each model, with by-participant random intercepts and slopes for the within-participant predictors and, where events or episodes were nested within participants, random intercepts for these units. Where this structure produced a singular fit, it was reduced stepwise, first by removing the correlations between random effects and then by removing random slopes. The structure used is reported with each model. Because the diagnostics (section 1.5.4) showed heteroscedastic or heavy-tailed residuals and non-normal random effects for several models, every test of a linear mixed model was repeated with cluster-robust standard errors (bias-reduced CR2 estimator, clustered by participant, with small-sample-corrected Wald tests;
Pustejovsky & Tipton, 2018
), which do not assume normally distributed or homoscedastic residuals or random effects.

For each model, pre-specified ‘main-interest’ terms (A and D, the questionnaire term of the across-condition form and the condition × questionnaire term of the moderation form; B, the event type × placement × questionnaire term and its interaction with condition; C, the questionnaire × prediction error, questionnaire × state error and condition × questionnaire × state error terms) were corrected for the five questionnaires with the Benjamini–Hochberg false-discovery rate (FDR), separately for each term, and are reported as q. Simple slopes and planned contrasts derived from a model are reported unadjusted. All p-values are two-sided.

The effects of instruction condition on net placement behavior were estimated with six models:
To examine how … / the effect of instruction condition on the net placement error relative to the hidden-state target, we estimated the model (M1):

log(|error| + 1) ∼ condition × (within-episode position + episode index) + cue + oddball on the preceding trial × condition + episode length + (1 + within-episode position + episode index | participant) + (1 | participant:episode),

which was fitted at trial level. Because oddball trials … they were excluded from this model (t+1), such that the error describes …  The model contained a random intercept for participant, random slopes for within-episode position and episode index, as well as a random intercept for episode within participant.

To examine the degree to which participants stacked multiple nets in a single location or distributed them across multiple locations within a trial, we computed the circular variance of the (up to) 7 net positions, cv = 1 − R, where R is the length of their mean resultant vector (cv ∈ [0, 1]). The circular variance was bimodal: on most trials the nets were stacked on one or a few neighbouring positions (cv < 0.10), and on the others they were split between distant positions. Because no unimodal distribution described this (a beta mixed model of cv did not pass the diagnostics described in section 1.5.4), the outcome was whether the allocation of a trial was split, defined as cv > 0.15, which for two equal groups of nets corresponds to a separation of more than about 63°; the distribution of cv has its minimum between 0.10 and 0.15. Whether the allocation was split was modelled with a binomial generalized linear mixed model with logit link (M2):
split ∼ condition × (within-episode position + episode index) + episode length + (1 + within-episode position + episode index | participant) + (1 | participant:episode),
which was fitted at trial level. The planned contrasts were also computed for the thresholds 0.10 and 0.20.

Furthermore, we examined the magnitude of change of the placement centre from one trial to the next, and how this is modulated by instruction condition, the different types of event trials (oddballs, episode transitions and outcome omissions). The change of the placement centre (shift) was calculated as the circular distance between the cue-offset-corrected placement centres of consecutive trials, in degrees. Because the placement centre did not change on 4.4 % of the trials, a constant of 1° was added before the logarithm, as for the error in M1. The model (M3):

log(shift + 1) ∼ condition + oddball + transition + omission on the preceding trial + condition × (oddball + transition) + within-episode position + episode index + number of oddballs so far in the episode + episode length + (1 + oddball + transition | participant) + (1 | participant:episode).

… the model comprises fixed effects of instruction condition and each event type, as well as an oddball–transition contrast per condition to examine whether the differential reactivity to oddball events versus the differential reactivity to episode transitions varies across conditions. Regular trials are the reference category.

Next, we examined whether participants transfer an episode transition shift observed in one cue to the second cue in the first trial in which the second cue occurs in the respective episode. This cross-cue transfer  was operationalized as the angular distance between two placements for the cue shown second in a new episode (|I_e|): its actual placement at its first appearance, and the placement expected had its previous placement been rotated by the episode’s 120° shift. The previous placement is the circular mean of the last three placements for that cue in the preceding episode, and |I_e| = 0° indicates complete transfer. The model (M4):
|I_e| ∼ condition × (episode index + transition direction) + number of trials of the first cue before the first trial of the second cue + (1 + episode index + that number | participant)
included … fixed effects … interaction contrasts … random effects … random slopes … and was fitted at episode level, with one estimate per episode and participant.

To examine how overall mosquito defense performance differed between instruction conditions and across the session, we fitted a binomial mixed model of whether a net intercepted the mosquito attack (M5):
intercepted ∼ condition × episode index + within-episode position + episode length + (1 + within-episode position + episode index | participant) + (1 | participant:episode).

… fixed effect of the level of instruction (condition), episode index, as well as their interaction, to test whether how mosquito defense performance varies across episodes differs between instruction conditions.   … random effects … random slopes …

The net placement error relative to the true hidden target at t0 to t+3 was modelled separately for episode transitions and oddballs, to investigate differences in net placement error patterns around the different events. An interaction effect between condition and trial (t0:t+3) operationalized how net placement error patterns around events differed across instruction conditions. The model (M6) was fitted as:
log(|error| + 1) ∼ condition × trial + (1 | participant) + (1 | participant:event),
with trial as a four-level factor (t0:t+3). Planned contrasts between conditions were computed at each placement.

Finally, we examined the effect of the level of instruction on the relative weighting of state error relative to outcome noise in trial-by-trial updating of mosquito net allocation centers. On each regular trial with an observed attack, the prediction error (observed mosquito attack direction – net placement centre) is the sum of two components known to the experimenter: the outcome noise (observed mosquito attack direction – hidden-state target) and the state error (hidden-state target – net placement centre). The change of the net placement centre from that trial to the next was modelled as (M7):
update ∼ condition × (prediction error + state error) + next-trial cue switch × (prediction error + state error) + (1 + prediction error + state error | participant).

In this parameterization, the coefficient of the prediction error is the weight on outcome noise, i.e. on the irreducible stochasticity, and thus the irreducible component of the total uncertainty. The coefficient of the state error is the additional weight on state error (distance of the net placement to the hidden-state target) beyond the weight on noise; the estimate is zero for a learner that responds to every outcome alike. All angles were expressed in the participant’s own frame (after removing the learned cue offset), and pairs in which the next trial showed either cue were included. The update, the prediction error and the state error were entered in units of 10°, which leaves the weights unchanged and avoids a convergence warning that occurred with angles in degrees. Condition-specific additional weights were obtained as simple slopes with emtrends (ref), at pairs in which the next trial showed the same cue.

To examine how internalizing symptoms modulate overall task performance and signatures of structural inference, we estimated four linear mixed-effects-models (A–D) per questionnaire scale (trait anxiety [STICSA-T], state anxiety STICSA-S], depressive symptoms [BDI-II], intolerance of uncertainty [UI-18] and obsessive compulsive behavior [OCI-R]). Model A asks whether questionnaire scores relate to overall performance, as a boundary condition for the remaining models. Model B asks whether questionnaire scores relate to the response to an episode transition differently than to an oddball, that is, to a displaced attack that does or does not signal a change of latent state. Model C asks whether questionnaire scores relate to the weighting of state error (i.e. angular error between the participant’s current placement and the hidden target angle) relative to outcome noise. Model D asks whether questionnaire scores relate to the transfer of an episode transition to the second (i.e. previously unseen within the new episode) color cue. Each model was fitted separately for each of the five questionnaires.
Each model was fitted in two forms. First, we fitted the models across instruction conditions, with the model containing the questionnaire but no condition × questionnaire interaction, so that the questionnaire slope is estimated from all participants, each condition contributing in proportion to its size. These models are estimated to examine whether a questionnaire is associated with the outcome irrespective of instruction (i.e. which information about the hidden structure was provided). Second, we fitted an extended form of this model, by adding the condition × questionnaire interactions. From these models, the questionnaire slopes were estimated in each condition, pooled over C1 and C2 (participants not told the structure), and as the two planned contrasts between conditions. In these moderation-form models, the questionnaire main effect is the unweighted mean of the three condition-specific slopes, in which the (current) 13 C3 participants count as much as the (current) 29 C2 participants, and it is therefore not used as the across-condition estimate.

To examine whether questionnaire scores are associated with overall task performance (Model A), we extended  M1 and M5 by the questionnaire (A1, error relative to the hidden-state target, A2, interception), with the questionnaire term added to the fixed effects of M1 and M5 and the same random effects (A1, A2, (1 + within-episode position + episode index | participant) + (1 | participant:episode)).

Whether questionnaire scores are related to differences in response to oddballs compared to episode transitions was examined across the first (t+1) and second (t+2) post-event trial. For each episode transition and each oddball, the net placements in  t+1 and t+2 entered the model,

Each participant was assigned the model with the highest posterior probability. Participants for whom random placement had the highest probability were flagged for exclusion from the analyses of the parameters. Because the exclusion rule is not yet final, the analyses of questionnaire scores and parameters are reported both for all participants with questionnaire data and for the participants assigned the latent-state model. The classifier was validated on 5,000 new simulated sessions (1,000 per model) by its accuracy, the expected calibration error of its probabilities, and the posterior probability assigned to the generating model. Because only the latent-state model contains placement noise, the comparison was repeated with a second classifier for which the three directed alternative models received the same placement noise (same prior and implementation), trained and validated in the same way; this classifier was applied to all participants, both classifiers were applied to simulated sessions of both model sets, and the model frequencies in the sample were compared by random-effects Bayesian model selection (

Validation of the parameter estimates.
Calibration of the posterior network was tested by simulation-based calibration (
Talts et al., 2018
) on 1,000 sessions simulated from the priors, with 1,000 posterior samples each, using the empirical distribution function of the rank of the true value and simultaneous 95 % bands (
Säilynoja et al., 2022

). Parameter recovery was quantified on 500 further simulated sessions as the Pearson correlation between true values and posterior means, the slope of the posterior means on the true values, and the correlations between the estimate of one parameter and the true values of the others.
Posterior predictive checks.

For each participant, the model was simulated with 100 posterior draws on the participant’s own trial schedule, and the 54 features were computed from each simulated session. For each feature, two quantities were computed across participants: the mean difference between the observed value and the median of the participant’s posterior predictive distribution, in units of the between-participant standard deviation of the feature, and the Spearman correlation between observed values and posterior predictive medians. The correlation was compared with the correlation expected if the model had generated the data, obtained by correlating one simulated session per participant with the median of the participant’s remaining simulated sessions. Bootstrap 95 % intervals were computed over participants (2,000 resamples).
Construct validity of the parameters.
Each parameter was correlated across participants with the behavioural measures that follow from its definition (twelve pre-specified pairs;
parameter_behavior_models_v4.py

), for example precision weighting with the mean net entropy, cue sensitivity with the learned cue offset and placement noise with the variability of the placements within a latent state. The behavioural measures were computed from the participants’ data and not from the model. The direction of each correlation follows from the definition of the parameter, and the twelve one-sided tests were Holm-corrected as one set.
Questionnaire scores and parameters.
The association of each of the five questionnaires with each of the six parameters was estimated with linear models at the participant level (
tambi_rq3_models.R
Questionnaires and Model Parameters

). The outcome was the posterior mean of the parameter, standardzied within the sample, and the questionnaire score was z-scored within the sample, so that slopes are expressed in parameter standard deviations per questionnaire standard deviation. As for the questionnaire models of RQ2, each model was fitted in two forms with the planned contrasts for instruction condition: an across-condition form,
parameter ∼ condition + questionnaire,
whose questionnaire slope is pooled over participants, and a moderation form,
parameter ∼ condition × questionnaire,

from which the questionnaire slopes were estimated within each condition, pooled over C1 and C2, and as the two planned contrasts between conditions. Terms were tested with F-tests against the model without the term (Type III with the sum-to-zero coding). For each parameter and questionnaire, three terms were tested: the questionnaire term of the across-condition model (1 numerator df), and the questionnaire term (1 df) and the condition × questionnaire term (2 df) of the moderation model. The p-values of each of these terms were corrected for the five questionnaires with the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure, separately for each parameter and sample (18 sets of five tests per sample), and are reported as q. Simple slopes and planned contrasts derived from a model are reported unadjusted.

The posterior means of several parameters were not normally distributed within conditions (section 2.3.5): cue sensitivity and placement noise were bimodal in C1 and C2 and concentrated near the upper prior bound in part of the sample, and precision weighting, belief momentum and the switch probability were right-skewed. The residuals of the moderation models were accordingly not normally distributed in 54 of 60 models (Shapiro–Wilk p < .05). The same three terms were therefore also tested with Wald F-tests based on a heteroscedasticity-consistent covariance matrix (HC3;
MacKinnon & White, 1985
), which does not assume normal or homoscedastic residuals.

The posterior mean treats each participant’s parameter as known. To include the uncertainty of the individual estimates, both models were refitted on each of 100 draws from each participant’s posterior distribution, with the outcome standardized by the mean and SD of the posterior means. The questionnaire coefficient of the across-condition model and the questionnaire coefficient and the two condition × questionnaire coefficients of the moderation model were pooled over the 100 fits with Rubin’s rules (
Rubin, 1987
), with the degrees of freedom of
Barnard & Rubin (1999)
, and tested with t-tests. The fraction of missing information of a pooled coefficient is the share of its variance that is due to the uncertainty of the individual estimates.
Instruction effects on the parameters and on behaviour.

The effect of instruction condition on each parameter was estimated with a linear model of the posterior mean (standardized within the sample) with the two planned contrasts; the contrasts were corrected with the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure over the six parameters, separately for each contrast and sample, and tested with HC3 standard errors as sensitivity analysis. To test whether the parameters describe the instruction effects found in RQ1, each RQ1 outcome was summarized per participant (mean log error relative to the hidden-state target on regular trials, proportion of intercepted attacks, proportion of split allocations, mean log shift after transitions and after oddballs minus after regular trials, mean |I_e|, and the participant estimate of the additional weight on state error from M7) and regressed, after standardisation, on condition alone and on condition and the six parameters. The planned contrast C3 versus C1 and C2 of the two models and the F-test of condition given the parameters show how much of the instruction effect on the behaviour is carried by the dimensions that the parameters describe. Because the parameters are estimated from the same behaviour, this is a test of description, not of mediation.
Incremental validity.

For the association of a parameter with a questionnaire, a linear model of the questionnaire score (z) on condition and the behavioural measures that define the parameter (markers) was compared with the same model including the parameter (F-test of the parameter, 1 df; change of R²; HC3 sensitivity). For belief momentum, the markers were the change of the placement centre on the trials after an episode transition, the slope of the recovery of the error after transitions and the error on the first placement after a transition (the participant-level counterpart of the association of STICSA state anxiety in Model B1). Because each parameter is a function of all 54 summary features, incremental validity can only be tested against a selection of interpretable measures.
Reliability.

The posterior reliability of each parameter was computed as the variance of the posterior means divided by the sum of this variance and the mean posterior variance, that is, the share of the between-participant variance of the estimates that is not estimation uncertainty. Split-half reliability is estimated by splitting each session at the episode boundary closest to its middle trial and estimating the parameters of each half with a posterior network trained on simulated full sessions whose features were computed from the same half (
split_half_networks.py

); each network was validated by parameter recovery on 500 simulated sessions, the correlation between halves was corrected with the Spearman–Brown formula (bootstrap 95 % intervals over participants, 2,000 resamples), and it was compared with the split-half reliability of one behavioural marker of each parameter computed from the same halves.
1.5.4 Model diagnostics
The assumptions of every fitted model were examined with the same procedure (
tambi_model_diagnostics.R
, called by each analysis script; all figures and values in
Model Diagnostics

). For the Gaussian linear mixed models, the conditional residuals (observation minus fitted value including the random effects) were inspected in QQ plots, histograms and plots against the fitted values, and summarized by their skewness, excess kurtosis and the share of standardized residuals beyond ±3; the homogeneity of the residual variance was assessed by the Spearman correlation of the absolute residuals with the fitted values and by the ratio of the largest to the smallest residual standard deviation of the three conditions. For the beta and binomial mixed models, whose raw residuals have no reference distribution, simulation-based quantile residuals were computed from 250 simulations of the fitted model (
Dunn & Smyth, 1996

) and tested for uniformity (Kolmogorov–Smirnov) and for over- or underdispersion. For all mixed models, the predicted participant random effects were inspected in QQ plots and tested with the Shapiro–Wilk test, and singular fits, convergence messages and the variance inflation factors of the main-effect terms were recorded. For the participant-level linear models of the questionnaire and parameter analyses, the residuals were additionally tested for heteroscedasticity (Koenker’s studentized Breusch–Pagan test), and the influence of single participants was assessed by Cook’s distance. The diagnostics led to four changes of the models, each described with the model: the shift in M3 was log-transformed with a constant of 1° instead of 0.001; the outcome of M2 was changed from the circular variance to whether the allocation was split; and the angles of M7 and Model C were entered in units of 10°. For the remaining departures (heavy-tailed or heteroscedastic residuals, non-normal random effects), all tests of the linear mixed models were repeated with cluster-robust standard errors (section 1.5).

2.1.3 Recovery after transitions and oddballs

The condition effects (level of instruction) on net placement error relative to the target angle (hidden-state target) after events was estimated with a linear mixed-effects model (M6), as planned contrasts of the condition means at each net placement. After episode transitions, the difference between conditions depended significantly on the trial (condition × trial F(6, 1618) = 15.48, p < .001) – on the transition trial itself (t0), placed before the first attack of the new latent state, net placement error did not differ significantly between conditions (C3 versus C1 + C2, 0.16 log units, SE = 0.139, t(235.9) = 1.16, p = .247; C2 versus C1, −0.08, SE = 0.127, t(236.6) = −0.65, p = .517). From the first net placement after the episode transition onward, net placement error was significantly lower in C3 than in C1 and C2, by an amount that increased across trials.

The model-estimated mean net placement error was 3.98 (C1), 3.80 (C2) and 3.14 (C3) log units at t+1, 3.53, 3.36 and 2.39 at t+2, and 3.82, 3.63 and 2.48 at t+3. Descriptively, the net placement center at t+1 had moved 0.24 (C1), 0.29 (C2) and 0.61 (C3) of the 120° rotation toward the new latent state, and at t+2 0.34, 0.37 and 0.79. In all conditions, net placement error rose again from t+2 to t+3. This rise coincides with the first appearance of the other color cue after the episode transition, which carries higher error than a repeat appearance of the first color cue (supplementary analysis ADD).

After oddballs, the difference between conditions did not depend significantly on the trial (condition × trial F(6, 2839) = 2.08, p = .052). Net placement error was lower in C3 than in C1 and C2 in every trial, including the oddball trial itself (t0, −0.81 log units, SE = 0.172, t(96.9) = −4.72, p < .001; t+1, −0.58, p = .001; t+2, −0.91, p < .001; t+3, −0.96, p < .001), and did not differ significantly between C2 and C1 in any trial (all p ≥ .093). 2.1.6 Summary of RQ1

On net placement error, recovery after episode transitions, transfer to the second color cue and the weighting of state error relative to noise, the effect of instruction was predominantly carried by the planned contrast between C3 and the other two conditions. The contrast between C2 and C1 was not significant on any of these measures. Participants told the latent structure moved their net placement further after episode transitions than after oddballs, carried the change over to the second color cue more often, and corrected their estimate of the hidden state more selectively relative to outcome noise.

2.3.1 Model comparison

The posterior probabilities of the five models were estimated for each of the 68 participants with the model classifier. The latent-state model had the highest posterior probability for 59 participants (87 %; C1, 21 of 24; C2, 25 of 30; C3, 13 of 14), random placement for 5 participants (7 %) and the model that covers both directions of each cue without inferring the active state for 4 participants (6 %). Neither of the two models that track a single direction had the highest probability for any participant (largest posterior probability of any participant below 10⁻⁸). For 66 participants, the highest posterior probability exceeded .99; for the remaining two, random placement was more probable than the latent-state model (.65 versus .35 and .82 versus .18).

On 5,000 simulated sessions, the classifier assigned 4,999 to the model that had generated them (accuracy 0.9998), and the expected calibration error of its probabilities was below 0.001 for every model. Its probabilities lie almost exclusively near 0 and 1, so that this validation shows that the five models can be separated on the 54 features when one of them generated the data. It does not show which of them comes closest to data that none of them generated. Of the five models, only the latent-state model contains placement noise and cue sensitivity. 2.3.2 Calibration and recovery of the parameters

children.label: 2.3.2 Calibration and recovery of the parameters

children.value: Calibration and recovery were evaluated on sessions simulated from the priors. In simulation-based calibration with 1,000 sessions, the rank distribution of the true value within the posterior remained inside the simultaneous 95 % band for all six parameters; the mean ranks deviated from their expected value by at most 1.4 standard errors, and the central 50 %, 80 % and 95 % posterior intervals contained the true value in 48 % to 50 %, 78 % to 82 % and 94 % to 96 % of the sessions. The posterior distributions were therefore neither systematically shifted nor too narrow or too wide.

Across 500 simulated sessions, the posterior means correlated with the true values at r = .998 for precision weighting, .988 for placement noise, .926 for belief momentum, .922 for cue sensitivity, .917 for the switch probability and .785 for noise reactivity. The slope of the posterior means on the true values was 0.82 to 0.99 for five parameters and 0.59 for noise reactivity, whose estimates are drawn toward the centre of the prior. In the range of precision weighting in which the participants’ estimates lie (1.5 to 3.5), the correlation for noise reactivity was .86 (206 sessions). The estimate of one parameter correlated with the true value of another at most at |r| = .21 (between noise reactivity and belief momentum). Within the posterior distributions, noise reactivity and belief momentum were negatively correlated (mean r = −.64), so that for a single participant a higher value of one is partly exchangeable for a lower value of the other.
2.3.3 Posterior predictive checks

The model was simulated with 100 posterior draws per participant on the participant’s own trial schedule, and the 54 features of the simulated sessions were compared with the observed features of the 59 participants assigned the latent-state model (
Posterior Predictive Checks

). For the 30 features that describe the level of a behaviour (means, rates and proportions), the mean difference between observed and predicted values had a median of 0.30 between-participant standard deviations, and the median Spearman correlation between observed and predicted values across participants was .76, which is 86 % of the correlation expected if the model had generated the data (median .91). The mean net entropy (ρ = .96; expected .97), the mean error relative to the hidden-state target (ρ = .92; expected .95), the proportion of intercepted attacks (ρ = .86; expected .93), the mean change of the placement centre from one trial to the next (ρ = .96; expected .96), the variability of the placements within a latent state (ρ = .92; expected .96) and the learned cue offset (ρ = .77; expected .89) were reproduced in this way. The fitted model therefore reproduced the differences between participants in the behaviours from which its parameters are estimated.

Two kinds of features were reproduced less well. The trial-to-trial variability of the behaviour, such as the standard deviation of the change of the placement centre from one trial to the next, was higher in participants than predicted by 1.0 to 1.7 between-participant standard deviations (four of five such features), while the ordering of participants was reproduced in part (ρ = .12 to .62). Differences, ratios and slopes, such as the change of the proportion of intercepted attacks over the session, were reproduced in value (median difference 0.57 standard deviations) but only partly in the ordering of participants (median ρ = .27, at 46 % of the expected correlation of .70). Within conditions, the rank correlations of the level features reached a median of 91 % (C1) and 88 % (C2) of the correlation expected within the same condition, but 63 % in C3 (13 participants), although the expected correlation was as high in C3 as in C1 and C2 (median .90); the largest differences concerned the error relative to the hidden-state target (ρ = .55, expected .86), the proportion of large changes of the placement centre (.46, expected .92) and the learned cue offset (.53, expected .88). A trial-level comparison located the first deviation: participants alternated between precise placements and discrete moves of the placement centre to the direction of the other latent state or to the location of a preceding oddball, which the model represents as a random displacement of the allocation on every trial (
Model Selection and Validation

). Accordingly, the median error of the placement centre relative to the hidden-state target on regular trials was reproduced (median difference −0.5°), whereas its 90th percentile was higher in participants than predicted (median difference 29°; higher for 93 % of participants).

2.3.4 Construct validity of the parameters

The posterior means of the parameters were correlated with the behavioural measures that follow from their definitions (68 participants; one-sided tests, Holm-corrected over the twelve pairs). Precision weighting correlated with lower mean net entropy (r = −.89, p < .001), a higher proportion of trials with stacked nets (r = .63, p < .001) and lower circular variance of the net positions (r = −.32, p = .004). Placement noise correlated with the variability of the placement centre within a latent state (r = .95, p < .001), and cue sensitivity with the learned cue offset (r = .71, p < .001), but not with the proportion of episodes in which the first placement for the second cue was closer to the new than to the previous direction (r = .05, p = .35). Belief momentum correlated with a smaller change of the placement centre after episode transitions (r = −.37, p < .001) but not with the slope of the recovery of the error after transitions (r = −.05, p = .34). The switch probability correlated with a steeper decrease of |I_e| with the number of preceding first-cue trials (r = −.31, p = .005) and, without surviving the correction, with the proportion of episodes in which the first placement for the second cue was closer to the new direction (r = .27, p = .013). Noise reactivity did not correlate significantly with the size of the change of the placement after oddballs (r = −.15, p = .11) or with its ratio to the change on regular trials (r = −.19, p = .061). All p-values are one-sided. Five of the six parameters were thus associated with at least one behavioural measure of the process they describe, in the direction implied by their definition; for noise reactivity, the correlations had the expected sign but did not reach significance.

The posterior reliability of the estimates (variance of the posterior means relative to this variance plus the mean posterior variance) was 0.98 for precision weighting and placement noise, 0.92 for cue sensitivity, 0.88 for noise reactivity and the switch probability, and 0.82 for belief momentum; within C3, it was lower for noise reactivity (0.55) and cue sensitivity (0.53), whose estimates varied little between C3 participants.

The split-half reliability was estimated from the first and the second half of each session (split at the episode boundary closest to the middle trial), with a posterior network trained for each half. From half sessions, parameter recovery on simulated sessions reached r = .996 to .997 for precision weighting, .977 for placement noise, .88 to .91 for cue sensitivity and belief momentum, .86 to .90 for the switch probability and .71 to .72 for noise reactivity (first and second half). In the 59 participants assigned the latent-state model, the Spearman–Brown corrected correlations between the halves (95 % bootstrap intervals) were 0.86 [0.74, 0.93] for precision weighting, 0.82 [0.69, 0.92] for cue sensitivity, 0.74 [0.55, 0.86] for placement noise, 0.73 [0.56, 0.85] for belief momentum, 0.72 [0.54, 0.84] for noise reactivity and 0.52 [0.14, 0.73] for the switch probability. For comparison, the behavioural marker of each parameter reached 0.88 (mean net entropy), 0.76 (learned cue offset), 0.70 (variability of the placements within a latent state), 0.37 (slope of the recovery after transitions), 0.27 (ratio of the shift after oddballs to the shift on regular trials) and 0.73 (rate of switches without an event). Belief momentum and noise reactivity were thus considerably more reliable than the behavioural measures of the same processes, whereas the switch probability was less reliable than its marker. Precision weighting (median 2.04 versus 2.38, Wilcoxon p < .001) and belief momentum (0.21 versus 0.35, p = .005) were higher in the second half; the correlations between halves are therefore lower bounds of the reliability of a stable trait.
The distributions of the posterior means were not normal, for reasons that follow from the instructions and from the definitions and prior ranges of the parameters.
Cue sensitivity.

In the model, the believed offset between the attack directions for the two colours approaches cue sensitivity × 70°, so that a value of 1 corresponds to the true offset of the task and any learned offset of 70° or more is represented by values near 1. Participants in C3 were told that attacks for one colour are offset by about 70° from those for the other, with an illustration adapted to their own trial schedule. All 13 of them had posterior means between 0.84 and 0.99 (median 0.96), and their observed learned cue offset had a median of 73°. Participants in C1 and C2 received no information on the colours, and their posterior means were bimodal: 23 of 46 had values above 0.7 and 18 below 0.3 (C1, 9 and 10 of 21; C2, 14 and 8 of 25), with observed learned cue offsets of 75° and 30° (medians), respectively. In the latent-state sample, the 95 % posterior interval reached the upper bound for 27 participants (C3, 10 of 13), so that differences between participants with offsets at or above the true offset are not resolved by this parameter.
Placement noise.

Placement noise was lower in C3 (median 0.18 rad, 10°; 12 of 13 below 0.4 rad) than in C1 and C2 (0.62 and 0.65 rad), where the distribution was again bimodal (13 of 46 participants below 0.4 rad). Participants with lower placement noise placed their nets with less variability within a latent state (observed within-state variability, median 24° against 40° in C1 and C2) and with smaller error relative to the hidden-state target (50° against 66°). The prior was bounded at 0.873 rad (50°), and for 11 participants (all in C1 and C2) the 95 % posterior interval reached this bound; these participants had the most variable placements (median within-state variability 45°, against 30° in the others), and their placement noise is therefore estimated with an upper limit.
Noise reactivity.

Noise reactivity was lower in C3 (median 0.33) than in C1 and C2 (1.70 and 1.37), and 5 of the 8 posterior means within 5 % of the prior range from the lower bound were in C3. In the model, a low value means that a displaced outcome is rarely attributed to an oddball and is instead treated as evidence for a change of latent state. Participants in C3 had been told that the attack directions shift by about 120° at irregular intervals, but not that single displaced attacks occur. Noise reactivity is the least precisely estimated parameter (recovery slope 0.59; section 2.3.2), so that values in the centre of the prior are drawn toward it.
Precision weighting, belief momentum and switch probability.

These three parameters were right-skewed (skewness 1.20, 1.26 and 0.97), without differences between the condition medians of a similar size as for the three parameters above. Precision weighting had three high values (3.6 to 4.9; two in C1), belief momentum had values above 0.5 for 12 participants (all in C1 and C2), and the posterior means of the switch probability lay within 5 % of the prior range from the lower bound for 6 participants.

Instruction effects on the parameters.

In linear models of the posterior means (standardized) with the planned contrasts (59 participants assigned the latent-state model), participants told the structure (C3) had lower placement noise (planned contrast C3 versus C1 and C2 = −1.49 parameter SDs, SE = 0.248, t(56) = −6.02, p < .001, q < .001), lower noise reactivity (−1.22, SE = 0.275, t(56) = −4.43, p < .001, q < .001), higher cue sensitivity (1.14, SE = 0.279, t(56) = 4.09, p < .001, q < .001) and lower belief momentum (−0.64, SE = 0.306, t(56) = −2.08, p = .042, q = .063; HC3, p = .007) than participants not told it. Precision weighting (−0.23, p = .47) and the switch probability (−0.30, p = .35) did not differ, and no parameter differed between C2 and C1 (largest, precision weighting, −0.56, p = .060). Instruction therefore changed how precisely and how consistently the nets were placed relative to the predicted direction, how fully the cue offset was represented and how readily a displaced attack was taken as a change of state, but not the expected rate of state changes.
Instruction effects on behaviour and the parameters.

When the six parameters were added to linear models of the participant-level RQ1 outcomes, the planned contrast between C3 and C1 and C2 decreased by 83 % for the error relative to the hidden-state target (from −1.62 to −0.28 SDs; with parameters, p = .12), by 89 % for the proportion of intercepted attacks (1.43 to 0.16, p = .40) and by 81 % for the shift after transitions relative to regular trials (1.34 to 0.26, p = .44), and condition no longer explained variance beyond the parameters (F-tests of condition given the parameters, p = .30, .70 and .60). For the proportion of split allocations, the contrast decreased by 36 % and remained significant (−0.88 to −0.56, p = .019). For the transfer of a transition to the second cue (|I_e|; −1.07 to −1.39, p < .001) and the additional weight on state error (1.97 to 1.42, p < .001), the instruction effect was not accounted for by the parameters (F-tests of condition given the parameters, p < .001 for both). The parameters thus describe the instruction effects on accuracy, interception and the response to transitions, but not those on the transfer of a change to the second cue and on the selective correction of state error.
2.3.6 Questionnaire scores and model parameters

The associations of the five questionnaires with the six parameters were estimated with the participant-level linear models described in section 1.5.3, in an across-condition form and a moderation form, in all 65 participants with questionnaire data and in the 57 of them assigned the latent-state model (C1, 20; C2, 25; C3, 12). Of the 90 tests per sample (six parameters × five questionnaires × three terms: the questionnaire term of the across-condition model, and the questionnaire term and the condition × questionnaire term of the moderation model), one remained significant after the Benjamini–Hochberg correction for the five questionnaires.
Belief momentum and STICSA state anxiety.

In the participants assigned the latent-state model, the across-condition model of belief momentum showed a significant questionnaire term for STICSA state anxiety (F(1, 53) = 7.45, p = .009, q = .043): higher state anxiety was associated with higher belief momentum (slope = 0.34 parameter SDs per questionnaire SD, 95 % CI [0.09, 0.59]; 0.076 units of belief momentum per SD). The association was retained with heteroscedasticity-consistent standard errors (p = .015) and when the uncertainty of the individual estimates was included by pooling over posterior draws (slope = 0.33, SE = 0.163, t(38.1) = 2.05, p = .047; 24 % of the variance of the pooled coefficient was due to the uncertainty of the estimates). In the moderation form, the slope did not differ between conditions (condition × STICSA state F(2, 51) = 0.01, p = .99; slopes in C1, C2 and C3 = 0.38, 0.33 and 0.34). No single participant determined the association: when each participant was left out in turn, the across-condition slope remained between 0.28 and 0.42 (p = .001 to .029; largest Cook’s distance 0.17). In all 65 participants, the across-condition slope was smaller and did not survive the correction (0.26, 95 % CI [0.02, 0.50], F(1, 61) = 4.50, p = .038, q = .15).
Incremental validity of belief momentum.

In a linear model of STICSA state anxiety (z) with condition and belief momentum, the standardized coefficient of belief momentum was 0.36 (p = .009; latent-state sample). When the three behavioural markers of belief momentum were added, it decreased to 0.24 (SE = 0.168, F(1, 50) = 2.00, p = .163; HC3, p = .217; change of R² = 0.032), whereas the markers together were associated with STICSA state anxiety (p = .039). Of the markers, the error on the first placement after an episode transition was correlated with both belief momentum (r = .45) and STICSA state anxiety (r = .36, p = .005); the change of the placement centre after transitions was correlated with belief momentum (r = −.52) but not significantly with STICSA state anxiety (r = −.20, p = .14). The association of belief momentum with STICSA state anxiety is therefore largely shared with the higher error on the first placement after a transition, the participant-level counterpart of the association of STICSA state anxiety in Model B1 (section 2.2.2), and the parameter does not carry information about STICSA state anxiety beyond these markers. In the model, this higher error corresponds to a belief about the active state that follows the evidence of the displaced attack more slowly. In the model, higher belief momentum means that the belief about the active latent state moves less toward the evidence of each new outcome, that is, that the belief is revised more slowly.
Further associations that did not survive the correction.

In all 65 participants, the questionnaire term of the moderation model of belief momentum was significant for OCI before correction (F(1, 59) = 7.04, p = .010, q = .051), with the steepest slope in C3 (0.83 parameter SDs per questionnaire SD, 95 % CI [0.15, 1.52], against 0.21 in C1 and 0.12 in C2; condition × OCI F(2, 59) = 1.78, p = .18); in the participants assigned the latent-state model, this term was not significant (p = .25). Higher STICSA state anxiety was associated with lower precision weighting in both samples (across-condition slope = −0.23 and −0.24, p = .064 and .067); with heteroscedasticity-consistent standard errors, this association was significant in all 65 participants (p = .009, q = .045) but not when the uncertainty of the estimates was included (p = .069). For the switch probability, the condition dependence of the OCI slope was significant before correction in all participants (condition × OCI F(2, 59) = 3.80, p = .028, q = .14), carried by the contrast between C2 and C1 (planned contrast of the slopes = −0.59, p = .038). For noise reactivity, cue sensitivity and placement noise, none of the three terms had p < .05 for any questionnaire in either sample.

The earlier analysis with partial correlations, in which each questionnaire was adjusted for the remaining scales, had shown a negative association between STICSA trait anxiety and the switch probability (partial r = −.34). In the models with one questionnaire at a time used here, this association was not present (across-condition slope, p = .17 in all participants and p = .52 in the participants assigned the latent-state model).

2.3.7 Summary of RQ3

Net placement behaviour was best described by the latent-state model for 59 of 68 participants, and by neither of the two models that track a single direction for any participant. The six parameters of the latent-state model were calibrated and recovered from simulated sessions with correlations of .79 to .998, and the fitted model reproduced the differences between participants in the levels of the behaviours from which the parameters are estimated. Five of the six parameters correlated with the behavioural measure that follows from their definition. Of the associations between questionnaire scores and parameters, one survived the correction for the five questionnaires: higher STICSA state anxiety with higher belief momentum, in the participants assigned the latent-state model.

Participant-level models of the parameters (RQ3).

The residuals were not normally distributed in 109 of the 120 models (Shapiro–Wilk p < .05), mostly because of the skewed and bimodal distributions of the parameters (section 2.3.5), and the Breusch–Pagan test indicated heteroscedasticity in 34 models (cue sensitivity, 20; noise reactivity, 11), which is why all tested terms were also tested with HC3 standard errors. For the association of belief momentum with STICSA state anxiety in the participants assigned the latent-state model, no participant had a large influence (largest Cook’s distance 0.17), and the across-condition slope remained between 0.28 and 0.42 (p = .001 to .029) when each participant was left out in turn. The largest Cook’s distance of any model was 1.03 (noise reactivity, BDI, latent-state sample).
2.5 Synthesis across research questions

The three research questions meet in the response to a single displaced attack. Instruction about the structure (RQ1) lowered the net placement error relative to the hidden-state target, increased the proportion of intercepted mosquito attacks, reduced the proportion of trials with splitted net allocation centers (WE NEED A BETTER WORDING FOR THE NET PLACEMENT SPLIT BUT IDK YET), increased the change of the placement after episode transitions relative to oddballs, increased the transfer of an episode transition to the second color cue and increased the selective correction of state error relative to outcome noise; the planned contrast between C2 and C1 was not significant for any of these outcomes. Higher STICSA state and trait anxiety and OCI scores were associated with a higher net plaxement error on the first net placement after an episode transition, but not after an oddball, and with a wider allocation after oddballs than after episode transitions on the first net placement after the event (RQ2, Models B1 and B2; retained with cluster-robust standard errors). At the level of the computational model (RQ3), the latent-state model described the behaviour of 59 of 68 participants, and higher STICSA state anxiety was associated with higher belief momentum; this association was largely shared with the higher error on the first placement after a transition, so that the parameter describes the behavioural association of Model B1 as a slower revision of the belief about the active state, thereby providing one possible mechanism of belief updating giving rise to the observed behavioral tendencies. The parameters described the instruction effects on accuracy, interception and the response to episode transitions, but not those on the transfer to the second cue (because the current inference agent shares the latent state across cues, so it has no individual dimension for transfer --> TO BE DISICUSSED IF WE WANT TO TRY TO ADD A SEVENTH PARAMETER BUT PROBABLY ONLY WEAKLY IDENTIFIABLE) and the selective correction of state error (BECAUSE IT IS NO SIMPLE LR MODEL).
